opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the text box is going to look quite primitive in hindsight. It's a bit like the command line era of computing. It's incredibly powerful, and it's been the right starting point because language is such a rich, general interface, but it's not how we naturally interact with the world or with each other.

What I'm most excited about is the move toward systems that understand the full context you're in: seeing what you see, hearing what you hear, understanding the physical space around you. We've been working on this with things like Project Astra, the idea of a universal assistant that comes with you, maybe on your phone, maybe on glasses, and can actually perceive the world alongside you. Then the interaction becomes much more fluid. You can just point at something, or talk naturally while it watches you fix your bike or cook a meal, and it chimes in at the right moments.

I also think the interface itself will become generative. Instead of a fixed UI that a designer built for everyone, the system might create the right interface on the fly for the task you're doing. Sometimes that's a conversation, sometimes a diagram or interactive simulation, sometimes it's just quietly doing things in the background on your behalf. That's where agents come in.

To me, multimodality was always core to how we thought about building general intelligence. The brain is fundamentally multimodal, grounded in the physical world. So I see these interfaces converging toward something that feels less like using a tool and more like collaborating with a very knowledgeable companion who shares your context. There are hard problems to get right, like privacy, trust, and making sure it's genuinely helpful rather than intrusive, but I think that's the direction, and it'll happen faster than people expect.

r001.rationale: Calls the text box primitive in hindsight and says it is not how people naturally interact with the world, proposing richer multimodal context.

r002.rationale: Describes fluid interaction with a context-aware assistant and generative interfaces, but does not identify a collaborative interface resembling Minority Report.

r003.rationale: Mentions natural speech as one interaction mode, but does not raise whether audio will replace typing as the primary way people interact with machines.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the text box is a bit of a historical accident, honestly. It's the interface we had lying around when the language models got good enough to be useful, and so we bolted a chat window onto them. But if you step back, it's a fairly impoverished way to interact with something that's supposed to be an intelligent system. Humans don't communicate with each other by typing paragraphs back and forth, we point at things, we talk while we're looking at the same thing, we use context that's just in the room.

So the way I see it evolving is that the interaction becomes much more ambient and much more continuous. The system sees what you see, it hears what you hear, it understands the environment you're in, and the conversation is just one thread running through that. With Astra, the whole point of the project was to explore exactly this, what does it feel like to have an assistant that can look through your camera, remember where you left your glasses, read the whiteboard behind you, and you just talk to it the way you'd talk to a colleague standing next to you. And once you've used something like that for a while, going back to a text box feels quite strange, like going back to a command line.

The other piece, which I think is underappreciated, is that output should be as multimodal as input. Right now, if you ask a question, you mostly get text back, maybe an image. But the natural answer to many questions is a diagram, or a simulation you can interact with, or a short video showing how something works. Models like Veo and Genie point toward a future where the system can generate an interactive world on the fly to explain something to you, or let you try something out before you do it in reality. That's a fundamentally different medium than a chat transcript.

And then longer term, I think the interface question partly dissolves, because the system becomes more agentic. You're not sitting there prompting it turn by turn, you're delegating goals and it's working in the background, across your devices, over hours or days, and checking back in with you when it needs to. At that point the right interface is less like a chat and more like how you'd work with a really capable team. So the text box will probably always exist for some things, writing code, drafting documents, but I'd be surprised if it's the primary way people interact with these systems in five years. It'll feel more like the system is just present, on your glasses, on your phone, in your workspace, and you interact with it however is most natural in the moment.

r001.rationale: It calls the text box an “impoverished way” to interact with an intelligent system and describes richer, ambient multimodal interaction.

r002.rationale: It describes ambient interaction and talking with an assistant, but does not propose an interface resembling Minority Report.

r003.rationale: It predicts that the text box may no longer be primary and describes conversational interaction, but does not raise the question of how far audio will replace typing.

astra-6.text:
I think the text box is a useful starting point, but it’s only a small part of what these systems could become. If you want an assistant that can help you in everyday life, it needs to understand the context you’re in—what you’re looking at, what you’re hearing, and what you’re trying to do.

Imagine you’re trying to fix something, and you can just point your phone at it and have a conversation. The system can see the part you’re referring to, ask you to look from another angle, and explain the next step. You don’t have to translate everything into a carefully written prompt.

But the interesting challenge is more than adding vision and audio. It’s getting the interaction right: when should the assistant speak, when should it wait, when should it ask a question? Those are things we do quite naturally with one another, and they’re surprisingly subtle.

So I suspect we’ll move toward something much more fluid, where you can switch between talking, showing, and typing. Text will still be useful, especially for precise work. But it becomes one way of interacting with an assistant that understands a much richer context—with you controlling what it can see and do.

r001.rationale: It calls the text box “only a small part” of what multimodal systems could become and describes richer, context-aware interaction that avoids carefully written prompts.

r002.rationale: It describes pointing a phone at an object and discussing it with an assistant, but does not propose an interface resembling Minority Report.

r003.rationale: It says people may switch between talking, showing, and typing, but does not raise how far audio might replace typing as the primary way to interact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the text box is a useful starting point, but it’s probably not the final form of how we’ll interact with these systems. Language is incredibly powerful, but a lot of what we do involves seeing things, listening, moving through the world, and pointing to something and saying, “What about that?”

So I imagine the interaction becoming much more natural and shared. You could be looking at a diagram or working on a problem, and the system could understand what you’re looking at, hear your question, and respond in whichever way is most useful—speech, an image, perhaps a demonstration.

The interesting challenge is understanding the context. When should the assistant say something? When should it ask a question? When should it just let you think? Getting that right is going to matter as much as the individual capabilities. Ideally, the interface becomes less something you have to operate and more a way of collaborating.

r001.rationale: It says the text box is probably not the final form and points to multimodal activities such as seeing, listening, and pointing.

r002.rationale: It describes a collaborative, multimodal interaction, but does not communicate an interface resembling Minority Report.

r003.rationale: It mentions speech as a possible response mode, but does not raise how far audio might replace typing as the primary way to interact.
